transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-22
Start: 15:30 PST
Duration: ~54 min
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE), Alice (CTO Helix), Marcus (Infra), Sofia (ML Platform), Jordan (Security)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive to validate HelmHealth's concerns around dedicated capacity vs hosted API for production throughput guarantees, noisy neighbor mitigation, KV cache behavior under warmup and burst, quantization impact on tail latency, and VPC/on-prem connectivity constraints. Team agreed to run a focused POC with three load profiles.

Topics: Dedicated v Hosted isolation, throughput fencing, KV cache warmup/eviction, batching strategy, quantization tradeoffs, VPC peering and egress controls, audit/KMS, fallback routing.

Transcript: [00:00] Evan: okay hi everyone thanks for hopping on i think we have about 50 minutes, quick intros?
[00:08] Alice: yeah i'm alice cto at helixhealth, thanks for doing this late, we wanted to focus on whether we should go dedicated or stick to hosted for our prod inference. our traffic is spiky and PII regulated so both perf and isolation matter.
[00:22] Evan: totally makes sense. priya i'll hand it to you to run through the runtime tradeoffs.
[00:27] Priya: cool thanks, hi all. quick note — i'll call out numbers as p90/p99 etc but our RL workload is chatty, many short prompts with average 16 tokens in request and variable response lengths. main things: noisy neighbor risk on shared hosts, kv cache hit-rate impact on latency, batching windows tradeoff for our latency SLOs, and quantization effect on both mem footprint and inference jitter.
[00:50] Marcus: when you say kv cache hit-rate, do you mean per-tenant prefix caching or global shared kv?
[00:55] Priya: per-tenant prefix + shared hot slots. on our hosted product we do per-tenant logical cache but it's co-located; for dedicated we can pin a KV cache set to a tenant's pool which removes eviction pressure from other tenants — this is what folks mean by capacity fencing.
[01:12] Sofia: important: our prompt templates are very repetitive, so we expect high prefix reuse. we care about warmup behavior though — first 10 minutes of a spike have lots of misses.
[01:22] Priya: exactly — warmup and cold-start TTLs matter. we typically recommend a short pre-warm phase for POCs to simulate expected reuse; also continuous background prefetch if you have predictive patterns.
[01:32] Jordan: security question — if we go dedicated on-prem, how does key management work? we need HSM/KMS integration and audit logs to feed our SIEM.
[01:40] Liam: for Private (VPC/on-prem) customers we integrate with customer KMS via standard keywrap flows and can support HSM-backed key stores. we also stream audit logs to your syslog/S3 per contract. there was a small note: on fully air-gapped installs we require offline key exchange.
[01:55] Alice: okay good. but our infra team is worried about network hops adding tail latency — VPC peering vs private link differences?
[02:03] Priya: peering is fine but you need to watch NAT and egress paths; PrivateLink keeps a shorter path. for hosted we recommend colocated regional endpoints to reduce cross-AZ hops. note: tail latency often correlates more with KV eviction and GPU contention than a couple of ms of extra network.
[02:25] Marcus: can you quantify GPU contention impact vs network?
[02:28] Priya: rough numbers from our benchmarks: under 80% GPU util, network adds 2-5ms; when util >90% you start seeing regenerated spikes — p99 can jump 60-200ms depending on KV miss rate and batching collision. that's why we offer throttling/fencing to cap tenant CPU/GPU shares.
[02:50] Evan: to add, hosted has autoscaling but multi-tenancy means noisy neighbors can still spike your p99 unless you buy dedicated pools or set strict routing policies. dedicated gives isolation but costs more and has commitment windows.
[03:05] Alice: our business needs 95ms p99 for chat paths and 250ms p99 for longer forms — is dedicated required to hit 95ms under 2k concurrent sessions?
[03:15] Priya: probably yes if your traffic is sustained. with dedicated and pinned KV cache + eager batching tuning we can shape p99 to that range. with hosted it's possible in a best-effort region but less predictable under cross-tenant bursts.
[03:28] Marcus: what's the overhead for quantization? we were thinking of 4-bit quant to halve memory. will that impact latency jitter?
[03:34] Priya: quant helps memory and increases effective batch capacity, reducing per-token cost. but lower-bit quant (4-bit) can add a small compute overhead on some kernels (dequantize/requantize) — on optimized runtimes we see 2-8ms extra per generation step but you usually get throughput wins that offset it. the big caveat: for small prompt/response sizes, quant overhead can dominate, so it's workload dependent.
[04:00] Sofia: we plan to quantize our offline models anyway. can you run a benchmark with both fp16 and int4 profiles?
[04:07] Priya: yes that's part of the POC. we'll produce side-by-side p50/p95/p99 and token-cost estimates.
[04:13] Evan: also we'll include warmup patterns: cold-start, steady-state, sudden burst; plus TTL/eviction behavior for KV cache.
[04:20] Marcus: on eviction — is there a way to pin critical prefixes so they never evict?
[04:24] Priya: you can pin, yes. for dedicated we provide stronger pinning and larger reserved TTL budgets. in hosted we can provide higher priority lanes but not absolute pin unless you buy reserved capacity.
[04:36] Jordan: security: audit logs retention — can we keep 2 years?
[04:40] Liam: yes enterprise packages support extended retention, but it affects cost; we'll include options in the docs.
[04:45] Alice: ok. another ops concern: what about fallback routing — if dedicated pool is saturated do you fail open to hosted? we need predictable behavior for patient-facing flows.
[04:56] Priya: we support policy-based fallback: fail-open to hosted, fail-closed (reject), or queue with backpressure. we recommend canary/soft-fallback where only low-priority requests route to hosted. we'll show examples in the rollout policy doc.
[05:10] Marcus: latency when failing over — do you warm the KV on the hosted fallback?
[05:13] Priya: not automatically. fallback to hosted will start with cold cache unless you replicate critical prefixes to the fallback tier as part of a sync job. that's an optional step.
[05:25] Alice: replication sounds risky for PII. does that duplicate data to another tenancy?
[05:29] Priya: it can be configured to keep data encrypted and only replicate hashed prefixes — we can also use tokenization to avoid direct PII transfer. Jordan we'll follow up on acceptable patterns.
[05:40] Jordan: yes, need to review encryption-at-rest and in-flight and tokenization approach.
[05:44] Evan: quick question from me — Helix wants 99.5% uptime SLA and <100ms p95. Are there traffic shaping knobs you'd accept to keep that?
[05:55] Alice: we can accept queuing for low-priority background tasks, but chat must stay realtime.
[06:00] Priya: we can apply per-route QoS: reserved throughput for chat routes, lower for analytics. On Dedicated we can carve GPU cycles per route; on Hosted we can do priority queues and throttles.
[06:12] Sofia: about batching — priya you mentioned collision — how do you choose batching window size? we need low latency but want cost efficiency.
[06:18] Priya: window sizing is workload dependent: for sub-100ms SLOs we use micro-batching (3–6ms windows) plus dynamic batching which expands when system idle. if you can accept 150–200ms p95 you gain large batching benefits. our Optimize tool suggests config per profile.
[06:34] Marcus: can we control batching at route level?
[06:36] Priya: yes, per-route configs: max batch size, max wait, batching strategy (latency-first vs throughput-first).
[06:42] Evan: i want to bring up KV cache eviction strategy — LRU vs LFU vs tuned TTL — which do you recommend for helix's short repetitive prompts?
[06:50] Priya: for repetitive short prefixes LFU or TTL-based pinning works well. LRU can evict hot prefixes if you have bursty unique sessions. we'll run a sim with helix sample traces.
[07:02] [10:12] Speaker 1: (inaudible) uh question about metrics — will we get token-level billing and cost breakdowns by route?
[07:10] Evan: yes token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route and per token type, with sampling and tracer hooks to link requests to traces.
[07:18] Alice: on the POC can we get trace dumps?
[07:20] Priya: yes, we can share flame graphs, p99 traces and kernel-level metrics during the test. we'll red-team the dataset for privacy.
[07:28] Marcus: networking — any special MTU or jumbo frame requirements for on-prem GPU hosts?
[07:33] Liam: not required; but for heavy KV replication and model shard movement, jumbo frames and high-throughput interconnects help. we'll provide a recommended network checklist.
[07:44] Sofia: let's talk about autoscaling — dedicated pools have min/max and burst policies?
[07:48] Priya: yes dedicated supports reserved baseline plus burstable extra capacity; burst can be slow-provisioned unless you pre-buy burst credits. hosted autoscaling is fast but multi-tenant.
[07:58] Marcus: is there preemption for reserved tasks when guests spike?
[08:02] Priya: in dedicated no preemption unless you configure it; we also support preemptible lower-priority slots to save cost.
[08:09] Alice: what about cost modeling — can you give rough delta between hosted expected unit cost vs small dedicated pool?
[08:15] Evan: we'll share a model but quick rule: dedicated reduces per-token variance and can lower unit cost at scale (committed utilization >60–70%) but adds fixed monthly reservation. hosted is pay-as-you-go with higher tail risk.
[08:28] Marcus: for the POC we need a realistic workload — we have 3 route types: chat-short (SLO 95ms), chat-long (SLO 250ms), batch-analytics (SLO 2s). can you simulate?
[08:38] Priya: yes we'll run three profiles including diurnal and spike windows; will measure warmup, KV hit-rates, and quantization profiles.
[08:45] Evan: note we'll use a sample of Helix traffic and we'll obfuscate PII before replay.
[08:50] Jordan: security-wise we need to review logs pipeline and retention and KMS integration.
[08:55] Liam: noted — sending security pack (security-pack.pdf) with network diagram and KMS steps.
[09:00] Alice: ok let's capture risks: 1) Hosted unpredictable p99 under multi-tenant spikes, 2) Dedicated higher ops and cost, 3) KV replication for fallback may introduce PII surface, 4) Quantization may change output quality.
[09:15] Priya: on quality regression we'll run evals against your prompt set; Redwood Optimize can flag regressions and suggest alternate quant profiles or mixed-precision.
[09:25] Sofia: is mixed precision supported? like int8 for some layers and fp16 for others?
[09:29] Priya: yes we can use hybrid quant: activations in fp16, some weights in int8 — that often gives a good quality/latency tradeoff. we'll include that in the benchmark matrix.
[09:39] Evan: last thing — runbook for failure modes? who will own failover config during pilot?
[09:44] Alice: Helix ops will own config but wants Redwood to implement the fallback and we both test it.
[09:50] Evan: great. we'll follow up with tasks and schedule. thanks everyone.

End notes: action items and next steps captured above. Shared artifacts referenced: security-pack.pdf (link shared in chat), capacity-plan.xlsx (will be posted), benchmark results folder (link to be created), POC contract template.

Transcript ends.
